_about: The repentance hub (plan 7.6f), built after love and righteousness. The review panel flagged it HIGH (committee-flags.json): שׁוּב simply means 'turn, return', so most of its ~950 verses are about going back home, returning a pledge or repaying, not repentance; and grouping repentance beside baptism and forgiveness decides a point (baptismal regeneration, sacramental penance, repentance as a prior condition) on which seven kinds of reader divide. So: (1) שׁוּב counts only where the verse turns to God or from sin, by hand, with the reason ('sense_keep'); the 800-odd other verses are left to the word's own card, and the builder counts them as 'other sense'; (2) 'a baptism of repentance' is its own noun row, as written, and 'repent and be baptized' is set beside 'repent and believe', 'repent and be forgiven' and 'turn and live', with no ordering of repentance, baptism and forgiveness; (3) God's relenting (נָחַם of God, 'the LORD regretted', 'relented from the disaster') is named as a different sense, in rows of its own, apart from a person's repenting, with the verses where God does not relent or change His mind beside them. A verse sits in every row it fits (match: all). The picked rows are by hand, as the divine persons are. Built by tools/concepts/hub_build.py into out/concept-hubs/repentance.json.

titles.verb: Who turns, who repents, and to whom

_words_why: The card's own words are שׁוּב (the Hebrew turn / return) and μετάνοια. Added: μετανοέω (the Greek verb, 32 verses), ἐπιστρέφω (the Greek that renders שׁוּב, 'turn to God'; also 'turn around' and 'return home', so it counts ONLY by hand, below), ἐπιστροφή (Acts 15:3, 'the conversion of the Gentiles'), שׁוּבָה (Isa 30:15, 'By repentance and rest'), ἀμετανόητος (Rom 2:5, 'unrepentant heart'). Two words the English also calls repent or regret but which are other words, kept in a row of their own that names them: נָחַם (grieve, regret, relent -- also 'comfort', which does not count) and μεταμέλομαι (regret, change one's mind; Matt 21:29, 21:32, 27:3, 2 Cor 7:8, Heb 7:21). They are never handed over as the same word as שׁוּב or μετανοέω. תְּשׁוּבָה (h8666, 8 uses) is left out: it is 'answer' (Job 21:34, 34:36), 'the spring' (the turn of the year: 2 Sam 11:1, 1 Kgs 20:26, 1 Chr 20:1) and 'return' to a place (1 Sam 7:17), never repentance.
_sense_why: The gloss rule keeps the verses whose rendering is repent, regret, relent, change one's mind. It drops 'comfort' (נָחַם, 62 of its 100 verses), 'change minds' (Exod 13:17, the people), 'relenting' (Jer 15:6, which the Berean reads 'weary of showing compassion'), and every שׁוּב gloss that is turn, return, restore, repay, answer. For שׁוּב and ἐπιστρέφω that is nearly all of them, so 'sense_keep' below names the verses that turn to God or from sin, one by one.

sense_keep._note: Every שׁוּב (h7725) and ἐπιστρέφω (g1994) verse that the gloss rule drops but that turns to God or from sin or is the LORD's turning with his relenting. Each is read in the Berean text. Left out on purpose: returning to a place, a person or a thing; restoring captives (שׁוּב שְׁבוּת); repaying; answering; the LORD's anger turning away (Ps 85:3, Isa 5:25, 9:12, 12:1, Jer 4:8, 23:20, 30:24) which is the LORD's side and not a person's repenting; turning away FROM the LORD (Num 14:43, Josh 22:16-29, Jer 3:19, Jer 11:10, 1 Kgs 9:6) which is the opposite and not this concept. Taken back in by the panel (2026-10-10): Ezek 3:20, 18:24, 18:26, 33:18, a righteous man turning from his righteousness, because Ezek 18 is shown on the wicked man's turning and the other half would otherwise look avoided; they sit in the warnings row with a note.

Hos.14.3.why: MACULA's Hosea 14:3 (Hebrew numbering) is the Berean's 14:2, 'Take words with you and return to the LORD'; the builder filed it at 14:3, whose text ('Assyria will not save us') has no such word

Matt.21.30.why: the Greek text MACULA follows orders the two sons the other way, so 'later he changed his mind' (μεταμεληθείς) is its 21:30; the Berean prints it at 21:29

others._why: Words the English renders 'repent' that are not this concept's own words (as love names φιλέω apart): named apart with their verses, never handed over as the same word.
others.title: Other words translated “repent”

_review: Not yet reviewed. The panel's flag (high): list only the verses where שׁוּב is turning from sin or to God, keep 'baptism of repentance' as one phrase, and set it beside the 'repent and turn' rows with no ordering of repentance, baptism and forgiveness; name God's relenting as another sense. Taken so; see the notes on the rows.

rows.label: The call: repent, turn, return
rows.note: In Hebrew שׁוּב is “turn, return” in most of its 953 uses: going home, back, restoring, repaying, answering. Only its turning to God or from sin is gathered in this section; its other uses are on the word's own card.
rows._why: by hand. A first try by the verb's mood (stance: command) took Exod 32:12 and Lam 5:21 / Jer 31:18 ('Restore us ... that we may return', a plea to the LORD, not a call to repent) and missed Matt 3:2, 4:17, Mark 1:15 and 6:12, which the frames file has no entry for. Hebrew and Greek together because the Greek Old Testament renders שׁוּב by ἐπιστρέφω and the New Testament calls the same turning μετανοέω; every example names the word it stands on. Includes the call as it is reported (Mark 6:12, Acts 17:30, 26:20). Panel (2026-10-10): the Hebrew Scriptures' examples lead (Ezek 33:11, Joel 2:12 first), and the note says what שׁוּב is: 'turn, return', of which only the turning to God or from sin is here

rows.label: Turn to the LORD, to God
rows._why: by hand, as the divine persons are: the verses where the text itself names the LORD, God, the Most High or the Almighty, or the LORD speaks ('return to Me', 'declares the LORD') or the prayer is addressed to Him ('return to You', Solomon's prayer, Ps 51:13). Those that say only 'the Lord' are in the next row. The same verb שׁוּב also turns away from the LORD (Num 14:43, Josh 22:16, Jer 3:19) and the shown verses are only the turning to Him.

rows.label: “Turned to the Lord”, to the Shepherd
rows.note: The text says “the Lord” and “the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls”; readers take them of the Father or of Christ, and the page does not choose.
rows._why: by hand, as righteousness's “He is righteous”: the text does not name the person

rows.label: Turn from wickedness, sin, idols, deeds; the repentant ones
rows._why: by hand, from a first try by the words standing in the verse (evil, sin, iniquity, deeds, idols), which had two faults: it took the LORD's own relenting 'from the calamity' (Exod 32:14, 2 Sam 24:16, 1 Chr 21:15, Jer 26:13, 26:19, 42:10, Jonah 4:2), whose evil is a disaster and not a sin, and it missed Ezek 33:14, which the frames file has no entry for. Left out on purpose because the verse does not say a person turns from something: Isa 44:22 (follows 'I have swept away your transgressions'), Neh 9:29, Rev 2:5 ('perform the deeds you did at first'), Acts 26:20 (deeds as the fruit of turning), Hos 5:4 (deeds that do not permit return), Zech 1:6 ('They repented and said ...'). Isa 1:27 ('her repentant ones', a participle with no frames entry) was a row of its own with Isa 59:20 and is merged here (consolidation, 30 rows to 25)

rows.label: Turn, and be forgiven, healed, saved, live

not_verses.Neh.9.29: 'by which a man may live' is the law's, not a promise made to turning
not_verses.Judg.2.18: 'saved them' is the judge saving Israel from enemies, and the verse is the LORD moved to pity (נָחַם), in the relents row
not_verses.Isa.6.10: says the turning is withheld ('otherwise they might turn and be healed'); in its own row (panel)
not_verses.Matt.13.15: the same text quoted: 'otherwise they might ... turn, and I would heal them'; in its own row (panel)
not_verses.Mark.4.12: the same text quoted: 'otherwise they might turn and be forgiven'; in its own row (panel)
not_verses.Acts.28.27: the same text quoted; in its own row (panel)

rows.note: Set side by side with the rows on baptism and on believing, as the text has them. Whether the forgiveness follows the repenting, the baptism or both is where Christian traditions part, and the page takes no side. These rows are listed in the order of their first verse in the Bible, with other rows between them; the page does not order repentance, baptism, faith and forgiveness.

rows.label: One sinner repents: joy in heaven; a brother repents, forgive him
rows.note: Luke 17:3-4 says forgive “if he repents”. Whether forgiveness waits for repenting is where readers part; verses that speak of forgiving with no mention of repenting are on the forgiveness card. The page takes no side.
rows._why: two rows of two verses each (Luke 15:7, 15:10 joy over one sinner; Luke 17:3-4 a brother repents) merged in the consolidation, kept as one by the panel ('fine as one row; the note should point to the verses on forgiveness where repenting is not mentioned'). The 17:3-4 verses are also in 'Turn, and be forgiven'

rows.label: They did not repent, would not return; Nineveh repented, Tyre and Sidon would have
rows._why: 'Nineveh repented; Tyre and Sidon would have' (6 verses) merged here in the panel pass to keep the row count down: Matt 11:20-21 and Luke 10:13 are the same saying (the towns that did not repent, and Tyre and Sidon who would have). Matt 21:32 removed (panel): its word is μεταμέλομαι and it stands in the regret row, named

rows.label: Repent and believe; believed and turned
rows.note: A verse that names both stands in this row and in the others it fits; the page puts neither first: Mark 1:15 has “repent and believe”, Acts 11:21 “believed and turned”. These rows are listed in the order of their first verse in the Bible, with other rows between them; the page does not order repentance, baptism, faith and forgiveness.
rows._why: by hand: Mark 1:15 has no frames entry, so no rule could reach it; and the rule on 'faith in the verse' took Luke 22:32 ('that your faith will not fail. And when you have turned back'), where the faith is Simon's and is not the call to believe. Panel: the label now carries both orders in the text's own words; Matt 21:32 (μεταμέλομαι, 'did not repent and believe him') removed, it stands in the regret row where its word is named

rows.label: Unless you repent, if one does not repent; a righteous man turns from his righteousness
rows.note: Ezekiel 3:20, 18:24, 18:26 and 33:18 say a righteous man who turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity dies; Ezekiel 18 and 33 also have the wicked man's turning (the rows above). What this says of one who is righteous, and whether it can be lost, is where Christian traditions part, and the page takes no side.
rows._why: the warnings as the text words them; what is warned of (perish, a lampstand removed, a sword) is in each verse and the page does not generalize it. The four Ezekiel verses added by the panel (Ezek 18 is otherwise shown on the wicked man's turning only)

rows.label: Repent and be baptized
rows.note: The text's own sentence (Acts 2:38), kept as written beside the rows on forgiveness and on believing. Where Christian traditions part on how repentance, baptism and forgiveness stand to one another, the page takes no side. These rows are listed in the order of their first verse in the Bible, with other rows between them; the page does not order repentance, baptism, faith and forgiveness.

rows.label: Turning others back
rows._why: Mal 4:6 added by the panel: the Hebrew source of Luke 1:17

rows.label: Lest they turn and be healed (hearts made callous)
rows.note: The text says it of this people: their hearts are made callous, “otherwise they might turn”. It does not say the turning happens. The page does not say why, and takes no side on what it implies for election and hardening, where readers part.
rows._why: the panel: these four said the opposite of 'Turn, and be forgiven, healed' and stood as its examples. Isa 6:10 and its three quotations are one text

rows.label: The LORD relents, regrets, has compassion (נָחַם)
rows.note: A different word and sense from a person's repenting: נָחַם of the LORD. It is not a verdict on whether God changes; the next row has the verses where He does not.
rows._why: by hand, as the divine persons are: the verses where נָחַם has the LORD or God as its subject, the Berean reading regret, relent, or (Deut 32:36, Ps 135:14, Judg 2:18, added by the panel) have compassion or pity. Exod 32:12, Joel 2:14 and Jonah 3:9 (asked or hoped, not said to happen) moved out to 'Turn and relent' (panel)

rows.label: The LORD does not relent or change His mind
rows.note: Set beside the row above, as the text has them; 1 Samuel 15 has the LORD regretting (verses 11 and 35) and not changing His mind (verse 29). The page does not reconcile them.

rows.label: Turn and relent: asked of the LORD, hoped for, and done
rows.note: Moses asks (Exod 32:12); the king of Nineveh and the prophet say “Who knows?” (Jonah 3:9, Joel 2:14); Jer 18:8, 26:3 and Joel 2:13 say the LORD relents when a people turns, and Jonah 3:10 says He did. Two words side by side: a person's שׁוּב, turn, and the LORD's נָחַם, relent. The page does not say what the relenting is.
rows._why: the panel: Exod 32:12, Joel 2:14 and Jonah 3:9 do not say the LORD relents, they ask or hope; they were under 'The LORD relents' as events. This row is the former 'A people turns, and the LORD relents' with those three, the label and note saying which is asked, which hoped, which done

rows.label: Regret, remorse, a change of mind (נָחַם and μεταμέλομαι)
rows.note: Two other words than שׁוּב and μετανοέω: נָחַם said of a person, and the Greek μεταμέλομαι (regret, change one's mind). Each example names the word it stands on.

rows.label: Every other use: turn, return, repent, relent
rows.note: Isa 57:6 is the LORD's “Should I relent”, another sense. At Deut 30:8 the Berean's “again” is the Hebrew שׁוּב, “return and obey”.

rows.label: A baptism of repentance
rows.note: The text's own phrase, kept as written (Mark 1:4, Luke 3:3, Acts 13:24, 19:4), beside the rows on repentance and forgiveness, and faith. Where Christian traditions part on whether baptism, repentance or both go before forgiveness, the page takes no side. These rows are listed in the order of their first verse in the Bible, with other rows between them; the page does not order repentance, baptism, faith and forgiveness.

rows.label: Repentance granted; God's kindness and patience lead to it
rows.note: “Grant repentance” and “everyone to come to repentance” stand side by side; in Acts 5:31 the text does not say who grants (the exalted Prince and Savior, or God who exalted Him). Where traditions part on how granting and a person's turning relate, the page takes no side.
rows._why: the panel: 'God grants' filed Acts 5:31 by an inferred reading (the Greek does not say whether the grantor is the Father or Jesus), and 2 Pet 3:9 is God's patience and wanting everyone to come to repentance, not 'kindness leads to it'. Acts 11:18 and 2 Tim 2:25 name God as the one who grants; Rom 2:4 'God's kindness'. One row kept: splitting it would make the two views look like opposing camps

rows.label: Repentance and forgiveness of sins

not_verses.Heb.6.1: ἀφίημι here is 'leave' (leave the elementary teachings), not forgive

rows.note: Set side by side with the rows on baptism and on faith. These rows are listed in the order of their first verse in the Bible, with other rows between them; the page does not order repentance, baptism, faith and forgiveness.

rows.label: Fruit and deeds in keeping with repentance; repentance from dead works
rows.note: The text's own phrases (“fruit in keeping with repentance”, “deeds worthy of their repentance”, “repentance from dead works”); where traditions part on how repentance, faith and works relate, the page takes no side.
rows._why: panel: Heb 6:1 is the works repentance turns from, not fruit that keeps with it; the label now says both

rows.label: Repentance and faith
rows.note: A verse that names both stands here and in the rows it fits; the page does not put repentance before faith or after. These rows are listed in the order of their first verse in the Bible, with other rows between them; the page does not order repentance, baptism, faith and forgiveness.

rows.label: Repentance, salvation and life; godly sorrow
rows._why: 'Godly sorrow and repentance' (2 Cor 7:9-10) and 'Repentance, salvation and life' (Isa 30:15, Acts 11:18, 2 Cor 7:10) merged in the consolidation: 2 Cor 7:10 was in both, 'sorrow ... led you to repentance' (7:9) and 'repentance that leads to salvation' (7:10) are one passage. 'Sinners called to repentance' (Luke 5:32, 15:7) was dissolved into the catch-all below

rows.label: “Impossible ... to be restored to repentance”; “no ground for repentance”
rows.note: Hebrews 6:4-6 says it is impossible to restore again to repentance those who have fallen away; Hebrews 12:17 is said of Esau, who “could find no ground for repentance”. Where Christian traditions part on whether a believer can fall away and what this verse says of it, the page takes no side.
rows._why: the panel: the earlier label 'restored to repentance' left out the governing word, 'impossible' (Heb 6:4), and so read as something the text offers; Heb 6:4 added to the row so the sentence is shown from its start

rows.label: Every other use: called to repentance, conversion (ἐπιστροφή)
rows.note: Luke 5:32 and 15:7 (sinners called to repentance, joy over one who repents) and Acts 15:3, which uses ἐπιστροφή, 'the conversion of the Gentiles'.

rows.label: Unrepentant
